sentences.text: The genus Aquilops was named by Farke and colleagues in 2014 and is classified within the group Neoceratopsia.
The generic name Aquilops refers to its beak-like snout, derived from Latin for 'eagle' and Greek for 'face'.
The holotype specimen OMNH 34557 includes a partial skull measuring about 8.4 centimeters, which is 84.2 mm long as preserved.

The holotype consists of a partial skull, a predentary, a partial left dentary, and unidentified fragments, and the known skull is 60% the size of adult Liaoceratops and Archaeoceratops holotypes but matches the size of a juvenile Liaoceratops.
The antorbital fossa of Aquilops is triangular and elongated, being twice as long as it is high.
In both Aquilops and Auroraceratops, the jugal bone is wider than deep below the orbit.
Aquilops was featured in the 2025 film Jurassic World: Rebirth and its associated promotion.
Aquilops is an important discovery indicating that Early Cretaceous neoceratopsians from Asia may have migrated to the American continent.
The only known specimen of Aquilops, a subadult skull, was discovered in 1997 by paleontologist Scott Madsen in Carbon County, southern Montana, within the Himes Member of the Cloverly Formation.

In 1997, an expedition led by Richard L. Cifelli of the Sam Noble Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, funded by the National Geographic Society, surveyed Lower Cretaceous rocks in Montana and Wyoming.

As an early ceratopsian, Aquilops is thought to have been bipedal, likely spending time walking on hind legs due to its small head and slender arms, unlike more derived forms with larger heads that walked on all fours.
Farke stated that Aquilops was a plant-eater that used its hooked beak to nip at vegetation.
While some researchers suggest neoceratopsians could eat meat, the shearing surfaces on their teeth were probably used for slicing tough plants.
Larger neck frills in derived neoceratopsians were likely used for display, while horns appeared only in more advanced ceratopsids.
One study identified Aquilops as the sister taxon of Sasayamagnomus from Japan, suggesting it is one of the most basal neoceratopsians.
Aquilops is basal to a clade containing the Chinese species Auroraceratops and the Mongolian species Yamaceratops, while Liaoceratops from China is more basal than Aquilops.

Aquilops lived in North America during the Early Cretaceous, approximately 109 to 98 million years ago, though a 2019 study by Michael D'Emic and colleagues revised the age of the formation to between 109 and 98 million years ago, while other sources place it in the Albian stage, approximately 110.1 to 100.5 million years ago.

The Cloverly Formation, where Aquilops was found, is dated to either the Albian or Cenomanian stages of the Early Cretaceous, and the Himes Member of the Cloverly Formation, the specific layer containing Aquilops, represents a braided river system.
The environment of the Cloverly Formation is poorly understood due to its unique faunal composition.
Researchers could not determine the exact age of the specimen through sectioning because limb bones, which are the most reliable indicator of growth stages, were missing.
The exact age of the Himes Member is debated among scientists.
It is debated whether the holotype's subadult status may have distorted phylogenetic results, as juveniles often display more basal traits.
Prior to the description of Aquilops, the timing of dispersal and affinities of Early Cretaceous North American neoceratopsians were poorly understood.
A 2018 analysis dated neoceratopsian teeth from the Arundel Formation to the Aptian stage, making them older than the Albian Aquilops.
